paras: The killing of Robert Stroud took place near Lake Village, Arkansas, in late March 1903, when a posse of fifteen men shot Stroud, a Black man accused of murdering a woman who lived with him, as he fled from his cabin. Struck by five bullets, he was taken by boat to jail and died there. Arkansas papers carried the story as a short state-news item, most often under the headline "Murderer Meets Speedy Death".

According to the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic, Stroud was accused of shooting to death Amanda O'Brien, described as "a mulatto, who lived with him," and beating her head, in the early night at a cabin on Dan Richardson's place two miles west of Lake Village. The paper said he then went into town, borrowed a Winchester rifle and ammunition, and returned to the cabin.

Stroud reportedly told a passing Black man what he had done and sent word that he would surrender to Mel Rankin "but no one else." When Rankin went out, Stroud stopped him 100 yards off and threatened to kill him if he came nearer, and Rankin, who had only a shotgun, turned back. Rankin then returned with a posse of fifteen men; the reports do not say whether he or any of them held office.

In the Graphic's account, Stroud was fired on as soon as he showed himself, and he ran back through the house and across a field "followed and fired on by all hands." He fell about 100 yards away, struck by five bullets, and was put into a boat and brought to jail, where he died during the night. The shorter version that circulated afterward said instead that he was shot down "when he tried to escape" and died "within a few hours."
No report of an inquest, a coroner's verdict, or any inquiry into the shooting appears in the coverage.

The first known report appeared on 30 March 1903 in a column of Arkansas news in the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic, which called O'Brien's death "a horrible murder" and recounted the posse's pursuit without comment. A condensed paragraph headed "Murderer Meets Speedy Death" ran in The Monticellonian on 2 April, saying Stroud "was himself killed while resisting arrest." The same paragraph was reprinted word for word in state-news columns of the Newark Journal and the Newport Weekly Independent on 3 April, the Malvern Times-Journal on 8 April, the Woodruff County News and the Columbia Banner on 9 April, and the Osceola Times on 11 April.

Every version treated Stroud's guilt as settled and named his race and O'Brien's, and the condensed text dropped the Graphic's detail that the posse opened fire when he first appeared. No coverage of the killing in the Black press was found.

The two versions differ on how the shooting began: the Graphic says Stroud was fired on when he showed himself and shot while running, while the condensed item says he was shot "when he tried to escape" while resisting arrest; neither reports Stroud firing at the posse.

reader.title: Killing of Robert Stroud
bases: A posse of fifteen men raised by Mel Rankin shot Robert Stroud, who was accused of murder and holding his cabin with a rifle, as he fled, before he was in any custody (A1, A2).

Stroud was killed by a group of fifteen pursuing him for an alleged murder (A1), but the reports describe an attempted arrest of an armed man who had threatened to kill Rankin and call the death a killing 'while resisting arrest' (A2); they do not say whether the posse acted under legal authority or whether the shooting was justified, so the papers do not settle whether the killing was illegal.

Only one account exists: the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic paragraph (A1) and a condensed version that ran in identical words in seven Arkansas weeklies (A2-A8); no independent report, inquest or follow-up was found.

accounts.label: Pine Bluff state-news column
accounts.gist: Stroud killed O'Brien, armed himself with a borrowed Winchester, offered to surrender only to Rankin but warned him off; Rankin returned with fifteen men who fired on Stroud when he showed himself and shot him five times as he ran.

accounts.label: Condensed state-news item
accounts.gist: Stroud was 'killed while resisting arrest': the posse went to his cabin and shot him down when he tried to escape; he died in jail within a few hours.

framing.detail: The condensed item, headed 'Murderer Meets Speedy Death', called Stroud a murderer outright and described the shooting as a killing 'while resisting arrest'.
The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic told the story as a 'horrible murder' followed by the posse's pursuit, without comment on the shooting.
